turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Friday, the twenty-third of October. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
Iran says it struck seven ships in the Gulf overnight. It named none of them.
[curious] None of them?
Not one. No flag, no operator, no casualty figure.
Mine's closer to home. Our air came clean yesterday for the first time this month — and the agency that measured it says the haze is back today.
And the spine of the book is the thing those two have in common. Not whether a claim is true. Who could check it.
[thoughtful] That's a bleak little thread to pull. Okay. The Revolutionary Guard said what, exactly?
That its naval forces hit seven commercial vessels. Four while they were transferring oil in the northern Persian Gulf. Three more set alight by mines, west of the Strait of Hormuz, the night before.
And the statement said they were burning.
All four were burning, in its words. It's the largest single-day claim since the war opened in late February.
With a threat attached, I saw.

If Washington keeps going, the scope of confrontation will extend to the aggressor bases in the region. Their phrasing. Central Command says flatly that no ships have hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz. It accuses the Guard of disinformation meant to frighten commercial shipping.
[skeptical] And there's a third voice.

The Joint Maritime Information Center, on an earlier claim, found there was no substantiation to these claims. And the American president posted that Iran is making up fake hits, mines, and everything else, to push oil higher before the midterms. It is. And here's why I wouldn't bank it either. The body that counts attacks in those waters — UKMTO — says of its own figures that it is struggling to accurately report true number of attacks. Because owners won't report them.
[drawn out] Oh, that's uncomfortable.
A missing incident report is weak evidence that nothing happened.
So both sides are standing on an absence.
Right. The thing that would settle it is very specific — a named hull, with a flag and a number, photographed with mine damage.
And until then?
Until then it's two assertions and no receipts.
What about the oil? That part's real.
That part's measurable. Brent rose three point seven per cent to a hundred and twelve dollars eighty-seven.
Which is the morning half of a very strange trading day, isn't it.
It is. Hold that — I want to do Singapore first. The National Environment Agency's six o'clock update on Thursday put the twenty-four-hour index across the island between seventy-one and ninety-six.
All moderate.
All moderate. First board of the month without an unhealthy reading on it.
And then the same page took it away.
The same page forecasts a hundred and one to a hundred and fifty for today. Unhealthy. Southeasterly winds.
[sighs] So we got one day.
One day, and it was a wind direction, not a result. Which brings me to the number I want you to keep.
Which is?
The Transboundary Haze Pollution Act came into force in two thousand and fourteen. In twelve years, no company has ever been fined or sued under it.
[pause] Zero.
[deadpan] Zero. Of six Indonesian firms served notices in two thousand and fifteen, two investigations closed and four are still open. One of those six is on this month's list again.
And what's the damage, against that?
An economist at a Singapore university puts this year's cost to the country at three point two to three point nine billion dollars.
And the maximum fine?
Two million.
[scoffs] Two million against three point two billion.
About one part in sixteen hundred.
Does anybody say that out loud?
A law professor does. There is no way Singapore can investigate and prove facts on the ground, he says. He expects action only against companies Indonesia has itself charged.
And the minister?
Asked whether the law has teeth, she conceded enforcement may not be so effective.
Which is a very honest sentence from a minister.
It is. Two opposition members will file questions in November.
What's the forum saying? That's usually where this lands.

That's my favourite detail of the whole page. The big haze thread on HardwareZone has passed thirteen thousand replies. Its standing poll on working through it runs seventy-two per cent in favour of staying home. But by Thursday the newest posts had left politics entirely. People were comparing microcontrollers for a do-it-yourself air sensor.
[laughs] They stopped arguing and started building.
One user weighing parts: the cheaper chip uses quite a bit less energy than the other one.
[amused] That is the most Singaporean response to a transboundary crisis I have ever heard.
Now. The money.
The strange trading day.

Thursday ran in two halves that pointed opposite ways. In the morning it was the oil shock we just talked about. The read was a central bank pushed toward more increases. One company disclosed its first cash outflow in more than a decade, and the whole artificial-intelligence trade cracked. The Nasdaq fell two point six per cent. The semiconductor index fell six point seven. The ten-year Treasury yield dropped seventeen basis points, to four point nine six per cent. Sharpest one-day fall since March of twenty twenty-three.
[curious] On a capital-spending disclosure?
On a capital-spending disclosure.
How do you know it was fear and not a rethink about rates?

Because of the shape. The two-year and the ten-year fell almost together — sixteen basis points and seventeen. The curve barely changed. A near-parallel shift is the signature of a flight to quality. If the market had repriced the policy path, the two ends would have moved differently. Claims fell by six thousand, to a hundred and ninety-four thousand. Near multi-decade lows. Hawkish, and completely ignored.
What did gold do? This is where I always get it wrong.
[wry] Gold did the un-gold thing. Middle East strikes, equity rout — and it fell two point eight per cent.
[gasps] It fell?
Because it's trading as a real-rate instrument right now, not a fear instrument. An oil-driven push to the expected policy path raises the cost of holding something that pays no coupon.
And bitcoin?
Behaved as high-beta Nasdaq. Down three point nine per cent. No catalyst of its own.
One honest footnote, though.
Yes, and I'm glad you asked. The global equity fund and the Straits Times Index both closed before New York's afternoon. Their falls are Wednesday's America, not Thursday's.
So the table would lie by omission.
Which is why we said so on the page.
[warmly] Good. Technology.

The Department of Homeland Security ordered every federal civilian agency to purge DeepSeek products. Here's the part that belongs in today's book. The signed order appears in the Federal Register only as scanned images.
[pause] Meaning what, practically?
Meaning the numbered paragraphs, the compliance deadline and the waiver procedure are not readable as text anywhere in the notice.
So the agencies bound by it —
— can read that they're bound. Not by when. And the accounts that carry dates disagree: one says signed in late July, one in late June, a third gives none.
If it's July?
Then the sixty-day window for an agency to object closed about four weeks before anyone outside government could read what they were objecting to.
[deadpan] Terrific.
DeepSeek answered the same week with code. It open-sourced the engine that runs its own production fleet.
And the hardware list?
[deadpan] Two entries. One American chip family, one Huawei chip family. That's it.
What did the developers do with that?

Inside forty-eight hours the issue tracker filled with requests to port it onto everything export controls actually leave people holding. It's a map. Home lab, quickly — a five-hundred-billion-parameter model came out last week, and people have it running on three desktop boxes wired in a ring.
[excited] Three desktops?
Three. About a hundred and three gigabytes a node, eighteen tokens a second. And a one-bit version now fits in ninety-six gibibytes — one box.
That's the number you've been chasing.
That's the number. And the sceptic line is the one for today: the lab quietly edited its own benchmark table five days after the internet started quoting it.
Up or down?
[deadpan] Up, by nine-tenths of a point. No comment, no announcement.
[wry] Still nobody told anyone.

The gear desk is the same shape. A pair of display glasses went on general sale at five hundred and nine US dollars. The maker's own page publishes no brightness figure, no field of view, no weight, no battery capacity and no runtime.
Then where does everyone get fifteen hundred nits from?
From a piece labelled, in its own header, a sponsored post.
[scoffs] Of course.
Fourteen customer reviews, all on the seller's site, and no independent long-form review of a retail unit anywhere we could reach.
Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every morning with this one.
What is it today?
Ultralight backpacking. Everything you carry for a week, in grams, minus food, water and fuel. That's your base weight.
And the line?
Under ten pounds is ultralight. Ten to twenty is lightweight. Over twenty is what the rest of us call backpacking.
What's the moment people fall in?

A former moderator of the biggest forum describes it. Ex-Marine, carried a hundred pounds in service. He says walking around snow-capped mountains with a pack the size of a chihuahua felt like having helium balloons strapped to his back.
[laughs] That's a great line.

The initiation is better. It's called a shakedown. You publish your entire kit list, itemised to the gram, and strangers take it apart item by item. Publicly. His own description: this is where you bear your soul — and then he corrects himself — gear closet.
[chuckles] So what do you buy first?

[amused] A kitchen scale. Not a tent. And here's the number that embarrasses the whole hobby. One writer put the two long-trail surveys side by side. On the Pacific Crest Trail, average starting base weight: nineteen point six pounds in twenty sixteen, seventeen point eight last year.
That's barely two pounds in nine years.
On the Appalachian Trail it went the other way. Nineteen pounds to twenty.
[gasps] It went up?
The gear got dramatically better. The hikers did not get dramatically lighter.
What does a good kit actually cost?
The sweet spot is four items — pack, shelter, quilt, pad — about eleven hundred and twenty-seven US dollars, six point three pounds.
And the high end?
Seventeen hundred and seven. So five hundred and eighty dollars to save one point eight pounds. That's about twenty dollars an ounce.
[drawn out] Twenty dollars an ounce.
And at the very top, one freestanding shelter costs about sixty dollars an ounce over its cheaper twin. The reviewer who tested it would not recommend it.
What's the culture like?
Very specific. Past ultralight there's super-ultralight, then extreme, and then a rung the forums call stupid light.
[deadpan] Which is a joke.

[thoughtful] It is not a joke. Their own ladder says that step can be fatal. The things people regret cutting are always the same three: a bear canister, rain gear, insulation. That's my favourite part. You don't buy from them so much as get allocated. One shuts its store entirely and reopens for a few days a month. One quotes October orders for April. One refuses a waitlist and runs a monthly lottery.
A lottery?
You have to answer a gear-knowledge question correctly to enter.
[laughs] You have to pass a quiz to give them money.
And a workshop on a farm in England builds to your measurements, with a policy that reads: all completed custom orders are final.
Can you even do this from here?
Honestly? No. We searched for a Singapore group, forum or club and found none. No local retailer stocks any of these makers.
[thoughtful] So it's a hobby you practise on leave.
[thoughtful] Which is the argument for buying once, properly. Every kit mistake costs a whole trip to discover.
Culture, quickly — what's moving?
A documentary out-earned a franchise film per screen by almost four to one. Three thousand and seventy-three dollars a screen against eight hundred and one.
On how many screens?

Eight hundred and fifty against three and a half thousand. It expands to more than two and a half thousand this weekend. Ninety-seven per cent — and this is the bit — from a hundred and fifty-six critics. Earlier reporting said a hundred, then ninety-nine, then ninety-eight. All true at a smaller sample. The score is drifting down as it gets more honest. A Swiss house made its first limited edition with an American footballer. Same price as the standard reference. To the franc.
[curious] No celebrity premium at all?
Zero. And you can only know that by opening two pages of the same website.
Family desk — what's the finding?
Sensors, not surveys. Every extra minute of phone after ten at night costs about half a minute of sleep.
So half an hour costs —
About thirteen minutes of sleep, and pushes falling asleep twenty-six minutes later.
And the honest caveat?
The cohort's average age is fourteen point eight. A twelve-year-old sits below the band that was actually measured.
Which almost nobody tells you.

The companion study is the useful one. The phone itself does relatively little. Getting a phone roughly tripled the odds of owning a social-media account — and that account, plus bedtime use, carries most of the effect.
So the decision isn't phone or no phone.
It's account or no account, and where the thing sleeps.
[warmly] That's actionable. Fitness?

Four minutes a day improved strength in seventy-four-year-olds. Real confidence intervals, published. The control group was a waitlist, a quarter of it dropped out against a tenth of the other arm, and the two groups didn't start level — there's a two-point-three-second head start on a two-point-two-eight-second effect.
[skeptical] So the trial flatters itself.
By design. And it still showed a gap worth printing. Both halves of that are true. General guidance, not medical advice.
And the closing essay. Give it to me.
Thailand. There's a kind of funeral mutual, and its benefit is denominated in other people. When you die, your family receives fifty baht multiplied by every member still alive.
[pause] That's not insurance. That's a bet on the headcount.

It's a derivative on national demography, sold to farmers. Ten and a half million people hold one. One Thai in six. Four hundred and sixteen thousand births last year — the lowest in seventy-five years. Five hundred and fifty-nine thousand deaths. Fifth straight year of more deaths than births. Two things move against the member at once. The cost rises, because you pay per death. And the benefit falls, because the payout is the headcount. In one province, a man holding three contracts used to receive about two hundred thousand baht. He now receives fifty-eight thousand. Fifty thousand to a hundred and fifty thousand. The product has crossed below its own purpose.
[thoughtful] Is it fraud?

There's plenty of fraud. But the argument of the piece is that the arithmetic came first, and the arithmetic makes the fraud invisible. If your benefit is falling seventy per cent for structural reasons, you cannot tell that from a committee stealing. And a committee facing a shortfall has every incentive to sign a thousand new members in a month. At three hundred baht a head, while already insolvent. Here's the line I keep thinking about. COVID didn't bankrupt these funds by killing people. It bankrupted them by selling to them.
[drawn out] Oh.
Membership peaked in twenty twenty. And the rescues raised the joining age — one association went from forty-five to seventy-five, then to eighty.
So the only people you can recruit —

— are the people whose deaths fall due first. The cure is the disease. America, eighteen sixty-eight. A fraternal order with exactly this structure: a dollar to join, two thousand dollars on death, and every survivor pays a dollar. One of them fixed itself. Brought in proper age-rated pricing in eighteen ninety-five. Lost twenty-eight per cent of its members in three years and disbanded in nineteen sixteen.
[sighs] The cure destroyed the patient.

And the part that makes it today's book: this is the country's largest life assurer in practice, and it is licensed by village headmen and overseen by a family-affairs department. No financial regulator has ever examined it. Nobody lied. Nobody was asked. The information asymmetry wasn't a flaw in the product — it was the product. By direct debit.
[pause] What's the test? If you're wrong, how do we know?

We printed it. By the end of twenty twenty-seven: fewer than forty dissolutions across both years, membership still at seven million, and no reserve amendment at cabinet. If all three hold, we were wrong.
That's the Briefing, then.
[warmly] That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-four pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
